tables.how: Condominium lottery: every building (block and lot) is followed through the 13 yearly result files. The yearly chance is winners divided by entries. "If every entry had the same chance" gives each entry its year’s chance and adds them up; the comparison uses the normal approximation to that sum. In the all-years row, first-try and long-wait figures use only buildings first seen after 2001, because the first file hides earlier entries; in the yearly rows the long-wait figure counts every building on at least its sixth entry on disk. Liquor licences: entrants and ranks from the State’s 2026 result file; the number of licences from the State’s announcement. Taxi: one row per offer letter; a driver is one list number.
tables.limits: The entrants are buildings of two to six homes, and their owners are private people: no building, address or owner is listed here, only counts. The lottery’s rule, as the inventory summarises it, gave ticket pools by years of owner occupancy; the ordinance text is not on disk, so the rising chance looks like the rule at work but could not be checked against it. The result files list buildings, not owners: one owner with several buildings would not show here (the aliases analysis tests that by address). A building marked a winner twice may have dropped out after the first win. The liquor drawing can be tested for one year only. Scored rounds, where entrants and winners are also known, are in their own tables because chance is the wrong yardstick for them. The aliases analysis (the site’s “One owner behind several names” page, "Drawings, licence lists and grant rounds") holds the test for one owner at several lottery buildings; it is not repeated here.

tables.how: Every application with a San Francisco address in the State’s applicant spreadsheets from 2019 (95 applications), matched by application number to the round’s award list. Of the 64 bond applications in rounds with an award list, 33 were funded: 1 of 21 in the first four such rounds (applications of February 2021 to March 2022), 32 of 43 since. The sponsor family is the parent company the State prints beside a general partner, as the analysis reads it.
tables.limits: The State’s regulations are not on disk. Its lists carry columns for set-asides, geographic regions and State credits, which suggests awards inside a pool do not go on score alone, and statewide such cases are common in the same files, so a "passed over" row is a question for the staff report, not a finding. An application may also have been withdrawn or found ineligible. Scores are self-scores or final scores as the State printed them. Rounds without an award list on disk show applicants only. A round in which every applicant is funded can simply mean money was not short. The swing in San Francisco’s results is set beside the statewide rate only as a yardstick: these are scored rounds, and had awards been drawn by lot at the statewide rate, 1 or fewer wins in 21 would come up about 1 in 16,000 and 32 or more in 43 about 1 in 210; a change in the scoring rules between those years would explain it, and the rules are not on disk.

Scooter firms are counted by the name on the applicant lists. Housing sponsors are the parent companies the State prints beside each general partner, pooled across every list that names the development; where no parent is printed, the general partner’s own name is used, and an abbreviation in a partnership’s name is joined to a parent only when a State row prints both. A development with two partners counts for both; 15 applications print no partner at all and are left out of the sponsor rows. An application is one entry in one round; "funded" counts applications in an award or recommendation list. Lobbying entries are filings in the City’s lobbyist directory that name the brand as client.
tables.limits: Repeat winners are no surprise in a scored round. The same few sponsors appear on most San Francisco applications in these lists, a site’s developer may be settled locally before any State application, and a project that loses can come back with a stronger application, as several in this table did. Scooter permits went to the highest scores. Lobbying is reported because the firms filed it; brand names are matched as words and one brand can be two companies over time. Sponsor families are read from names: two partnerships with similar names may be unrelated.

tables.how: 64 pools with two or more members and enough spending to compare were found in Public Works’ monthly status reports, the Port’s contracting reports and the City’s contract file. In 17 of them one member took half or more of a pool of three or more, the most lopsided being Lee Incorporated with 81.3% of $7.1 million in "PUC Speclzed Tech AsNeeded Srv" (Public Utilities Commission; the pool name is the contract title as the City’s file abbreviates it). 26 member places across these pools show no spending at all. In Public Works’ own reports the widest gap is Smith-Emery San Francisco at 69.8% of "Special Inspection & Testing", against an even share of 20%. Neither department’s quoted rule promises rotation or an even split. Public Works: the status report for the month ending 31 October 2026 gives each pool member’s master contract amount and amount expended to date. Members of one pool are grouped by contract generation (contracts ending within 300 days of each other); job-order contracts, which are separate contracts for one kind of work, are grouped by trade. Port: payments per contract in each fiscal year’s contracting report (fiscal 2016-17, first half of fiscal 2017-18, fiscal 2018-19, fiscal 2019-20, fiscal 2020-21, fiscal 2021-22), added up for the four pools whose tables parse cleanly. Other departments: contract titles in the City’s contract file that contain "as-needed", "pool", "on-call", "job order" or "master agreement" with three or more prime contractors and $1 million or more paid, as in the aliases analysis. An even share is one divided by the number of members; "times an even share" divides the largest member’s share by it. "JV" in a member’s name is the record’s short form for a joint venture. The owner-groups built by the aliases analysis were used to count sister companies as one entrant.
tables.limits: What the rules say, as quoted in the download: Public Works, “Work will be authorized through individual Contract Service Orders based on project needs and available funding.”; Port, “Staff initiate a CSO to meet a specific need and the prime then forms a team, pulling from the subconsultants assembled at time of proposal.” Nothing quoted requires rotation, so an uneven split breaks no rule shown here. Uneven shares have ordinary causes: members were awarded contracts of different sizes (the capacity column shows the largest member’s share of the pool’s contract value), specialties differ inside one pool, a member may decline work, and one large project can absorb a contract. No department publishes a log of task orders (both call them Contract Service Orders), so the number and size of individual orders cannot be seen. Public Works figures are cumulative and a few fell from one month to the next, which suggests corrections. Port names are as printed, so one firm under two different names appears twice. Newly awarded generations with under $500,000 spent are left out as too young to judge. In the City’s contract file a zero means no payment is recorded, and members whose contracts began later have had less time to be paid.

Public Works: amount expended to date and master contract amount from the status report; Port: payments added over the report years; other departments: every line of the City’s contract file under the pool’s contract title, payments and agreed amounts added up per prime contractor (the file’s lines for team members are credited to their prime, as the analysis counts them).
tables.limits: What the rules say, as quoted in the download: Public Works, “Work will be authorized through individual Contract Service Orders based on project needs and available funding.”; Port, “Staff initiate a CSO to meet a specific need and the prime then forms a team, pulling from the subconsultants assembled at time of proposal.” Nothing quoted requires rotation, so an uneven split breaks no rule shown here. Uneven shares have ordinary causes: members were awarded contracts of different sizes (the capacity column shows the largest member’s share of the pool’s contract value), specialties differ inside one pool, a member may decline work, and one large project can absorb a contract. No department publishes a log of task orders (both call them Contract Service Orders), so the number and size of individual orders cannot be seen. Public Works figures are cumulative and a few fell from one month to the next, which suggests corrections. Port names are as printed, so one firm under two different names appears twice. Newly awarded generations with under $500,000 spent are left out as too young to judge. In the City’s contract file a zero means no payment is recorded, and members whose contracts began later have had less time to be paid.

tables.how: Housing credits: 11 times one parent company stood behind two or more separately named applicants in the same State round, the most being 4. Community grants: San Francisco Parks Alliance was the fiscal sponsor of 11 of the 19 awards in fiscal 2022, and of 27 awards worth $2.3 million over the four award years on disk. Public Works pools: in 14 cases (10 firms) a firm holds its own contract in a pool and also sits on another member’s team in the same pool. Owner-groups from the aliases analysis tie 2 sets of differently named winners in one round. The 2026 liquor lists, where the State accepts one application per applicant, show no two entrants sharing a registered owner account or business address. Four tests. (1) State tax-credit rounds: applicants are single-project partnerships, and the State prints each general partner’s parent company; applications in one round are grouped by parent. (2) Community Challenge Grants: awards whose grantee line reads "sponsored by" are grouped by sponsor within the award year. (3) Public Works pools: each pool contract number in the status report is looked up in the City’s contract file, which lists joint-venture members and subcontractors; a firm counts when it holds its own contract in the pool and is on another member’s team in the same pool. (4) Every round and pool is checked against the owner-groups; the liquor entrants and storefront-grant recipients are also looked up in the City’s business registry by exact name and compared by business address. The owner-groups built by the aliases analysis were used to count sister companies as one entrant.
tables.limits: None of this is shown to break a rule, and most of it is how the programs are built. In the State’s lists every development applies through its own partnership, so one developer appears under several names; the State prints the parent beside each, so nothing is hidden. A group listed as "sponsored by" another organization applied through that organization; the award pages do not say what the sponsor keeps or controls. Pool contracts carry local-business subcontracting goals (the Port’s reports print the goal beside each contract), an ordinary reason for members to hire one another; whether a firm may be both a member and another member’s subcontractor is set by each solicitation, which is not on disk. The Art Vendor program’s own evaluation says “The current lottery system creates inequitable outcomes as family unit members are permitted to enter the lottery as individuals.”; the licence list carries no household information, so that could not be tested. Registry matching is by exact name and misses businesses registered under another name. Team lists come from the City’s contract file and may be incomplete.

tables.how: 20 organizations and firms appear as a winner or member in two or more different places. 4 of the 8 entrants in the 2026 neighborhood liquor-licence drawing are also on the 2026 Storefront Opportunity Grant list (4 joined through the business registry, not by name alone), 2 of them ranked within the licences available; 3 firms hold places in three or more Public Works pools at once; 13 organizations won in more than one grant or credit program. 9 of them are profiled City payees and 7 have staff recorded as campaign donors. A "place" is one program: the State liquor drawing, the Storefront Opportunity Grant, Community Challenge Grants, Arts Commission grants (the two files count as one program), State housing credits, or one Public Works pool. Names are matched by exact normalised name or shared owner-group. Liquor entrants and storefront recipients are joined through the City’s business registry: the grant’s business address must be a registered location of the entrant’s owner name, or the names must be the same. City payments, staff donations and lobbying come from this project’s profiles of City-funded organizations. 2 rows of the storefront table had a business name split by a number in it; the stray part was put back before matching.
tables.limits: Unless a row says "Registry" or "Owner-group", it is a name match and two bodies can share a name. The liquor licences are limited to specified census tracts and all 4 matches are listed by the grant program under Bayview, so a new restaurant there could naturally seek both a grant and a licence; an arts organization that runs a neighborhood project fits two grant programs; and an engineering firm with several specialties can qualify for several pools. Donations by an organization’s staff are personal donations, matched by the employer the donor wrote down. The profiles cover City-funded nonprofits, so firms show no payment figure here even when the City pays them.

tables.how: 74 listings on the City’s housing portal offered 689 homes and drew 128,010 applications; the middle listing had 260 applications per home and the most contested 2,925. Holders of a Certificate of Preference filed 0.44 applications for each home open to them, and in 50 of 74 listings there were at least as many such homes as certificate applicants; live-or-work applicants filed 101 per home. In every one of the 74 listings applicants with no preference could not reach a home by arithmetic, because applicants holding a preference alone outnumbered the homes. One row per listing that has preference counts in the portal’s data. Applications are the live-or-work count plus the general pool, which together match the number of tickets printed in the results files to within 1%. Each preference’s figure is its applications divided by the homes open to it. "Left for live-or-work applicants" takes the homes and subtracts, in the order the portal lists them, the smaller of each earlier preference’s applications and its reserved homes; "left for no preference" subtracts the live-or-work applications as well. Listings named only by a street address with fewer than five homes are not identified. 33 listings are named only by a street address with fewer than five homes and are not identified.
tables.limits: These are counts of applications, not people housed: results files list ticket numbers, and the portal data shows only the top ticket in each preference, so who was actually placed is not public. The arithmetic assumes every preference applicant qualifies and accepts, which overstates how many homes preferences take: the Budget and Legislative Analyst’s 2022 report (in the reviews table) found many applications were being reviewed for each home filled. One household can hold several preferences and is counted in each. The portal exposes only listings still live, mostly from 2025 and 2026. Preferences are the program’s published rules. The rule: “there is no separate drawing for each pool, applicants receive only one lottery rank number which determines their position on each preference list.”

tables.how: Taxi medallions: free medallions went down a waiting list that held 3,029 people in 2012, by when it was closed to new names; from 2010 the City offered medallions for sale instead. Of 722 medallions now held as purchased, 302 (41.8%) are marked foreclosed, and 302 purchased medallions are held in the name of 2 credit unions, so the buyers are not shown to have gained. Condominium lottery: 199 homes a year won conversion until 2013, when 593 entered buildings lost the last drawing; the fee-based program that replaced it converted 1,915 homes, 1,155 of them in its first year, by eligibility and fee, with no drawing. Taxi: offer letters are counted by year from the archived notices; current medallions by holder type, last sale price and financial status from the transportation agency’s holder file (holder types are the file’s own labels). Condominiums: homes in winning buildings per lottery year; homes converted under the replacement program are read from the table in Public Works’ report of 29 December 2023. Drivers and building owners are counted, never named.
tables.limits: Who gained is only partly visible. The records do not show what sellers received, what the City collected, or which waiting-list members bought. A foreclosed medallion is a loss to its buyer and lender, not proof the rule was wrong when made. The courts: “Appeal Court affirms trial court verdict that City did not breach its contract with credit union in taxi medallion case” For condominiums the records do not link lottery losers to later conversions, so it cannot be said that the same owners moved from the drawing to the paid program. Public Works’ report says the ordinance “established seven application rounds each of which had different eligibility date requirements”; those requirements are not on disk, so who qualified first cannot be stated. Its 2019 update says “no lottery shall take place prior to January 1, 2024” and that the longest suspension would be found by “dividing the total number of units approved for conversion in the ECP by 200 and rounded to the nearest whole number”, added to 2014. No lottery result after 2013 is on disk, so whether drawings resumed is not known here.
